report:
The family has moved from open conflict to a shared list of concerns and a plan of information-gathering, with no decision made on price.

Where things stand:

The will and the estate are still unknown. None of the three sisters knows who holds the will or who is the executor. They have each taken one enquiry: C is checking their dad's papers at home, A is contacting the solicitor and any will register, and B is contacting the bank and other financial institutions. All three accepted a two-week target for these enquiries, and all three were clear it is a target for gathering information, not a deadline for a decision.

The list of concerns, agreed by all three, covers nine items: finding and reading the will; establishing the estate's assets and debts; an independent valuation of the house before any discount is discussed; B speaking for herself; any discount coming only out of A's own share; the separate and still open question of whether there is a discount at all; target dates so an empty house does not drain the estate; written terms checked by a lawyer before signing; the work not falling on one sister alone; and no price or option agreed before the will and valuation are in hand.

The main shift is on the price question. A first asked to buy at a family discount, which C refused. A has now said a discount means she uses her own share toward the house and pays B and C for theirs, not that they accept less than their share is worth. C and B both said they would accept A buying at the full independent valuation in principle. So all three now agree no sister should receive less than her share is worth. The one open practical question is whether A and her husband can raise two thirds of the valuation.

I corrected myself once. I had said the discount question was settled when A offered to fund a discount from her own share. C rightly disagreed, and the list now separates the funding rule from the question of whether a discount happens at all.

Nothing has been signed and no money has moved. I gave no legal, tax, or mortgage advice, and I told the family each time that a lawyer and a lender are needed for those parts. The next real step is theirs: the three enquiries, then the will, then the valuation, and only then a price for A to test against the list.
